title: Age-related preference for geometric spatial cues during real-world navigation
research_question: How do geometry and landmark cues control navigation in young and older adults in a real, ecological environment, and what are the oculomotor signatures of landmark- versus geometry-related spatial coding?

participants.description: 20 young adults (19-37 years, mean 26.25, 11 females, 9 males) and 19 older adults (61-81 years, mean 72.2, 10 females, 9 males) from Paris, France. All participants were clinically and functionally screened to ensure normal visual, audio-vestibular, postural, oculomotor, and cognitive characteristics.
participants.recruitment: Participants were recruited from the SilverSight cohort population at the Vision Institute-Quinze-Vingts National Ophthalmology Centre, Paris. They were voluntary and received financial compensation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A real street-like, open-field maze (Streetlab platform) consisting of a rectangular enclosure (8.55 × 4.30 m²) with 19 wall panels providing real-world textures (e.g., brick walls, doors, windows). The floor was black linoleum. Homogeneous illumination (195 lux) and street-like multi-source sounds were provided. An unmarked goal zone (80 × 80 cm²) was used. A conflict between landmark and geometric cues was introduced by rotating the entire array of wall panels.

measures.instrument: First area entered (G, S, L, or E) based on subject's trajectory during probe trial
Time from eye opening to movement initiation
Ratio of trajectory length to shortest distance to goal
Mean angular error of momentary velocity vectors relative to goal
Entering symmetric corner (S) before goal (G) during learning/probe trials
Eye-tracker recordings (fixation frequency, duration, interfixation distance, altitude, explorative/exploitative fixations, surface area covered)

Battery of tests: Mental Rotation (MR), Mental Flexibility (FLEX), Visual Memory (FGT1-3), Spatial Memory (CORSI1-2), Inhibition (INHIB), Perspective-Taking (PERSP), Visual Acuity (VAD, VAL), Useful Field of View (UFOV1-3), Visual Field (VF), Contrast Sensitivity (CS1-6)
Head and trunk orientations (yaw, pitch) from motion capture

findings.consequent: Preference for geometric cues in navigation
findings.mechanism: Navigation difficulties in aged people are associated with deficits in processing and encoding spatial cues.
findings.quote: a majority of older subjects reoriented and navigated according to the geometry of the environment... significant difference in the proportion of subjects who oriented based on geometry across the two age groups (χ²=5.77, P<0.02)
a majority of young adults reoriented and navigated to the goal based on the environmental landmarks
No significant gender effect was found (χ² = 1.43, P=0.23, odds ratio = 0.45, odds ratio 95% CI 0.12-1.67)

findings.consequent: Mean group trajectory deviation with respect to goal location
findings.mechanism: Reliance on geometric cues leads to more direct path to goal G or S.
findings.quote: a statistically significant deviation of the mean group trajectory with respect to the goal location or its symmetric location (F(1,35)=46.66, P<0.001, partial η² = 0.57, η² 95% CI 0.33–0.70)

findings.consequent: Time spent in goal zone G
findings.quote: Cue preference was also reflected in the time spent by the geometry and landmark groups in zones G and L, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2).

findings.mechanism: Reflects an unbalanced exploration-exploitation trade-off in scanning policies.
findings.quote: older subjects spent a significantly longer time in reorienting across all learning trials (F(1,35) = 47.41, P<0.001, partial η² = 0.57, η² 95% CI0.33–0.7)
they walked at a significantly slower speed (F(1,35) = 13.47, P<0.001, partial η² = 0.28, η² 95% CI 0.05-0.47)
they travelled a longer and a more tortuous path to the goal (distance: F(1,35)=15.40, P<0.001, partial η² = 0.30, η² 95% CI 0.07–0.49)
path tortuosity: F(1, 35) = 13.95; P<0.001, partial η²=0.28, η² 95% CI 0.06–0.48
heading deviation: F(1,35)=7.77, P<0.01, partial η²=0.18, η² 95% CI 0.01-0.38
it required longer for older subjects to reach the goal location (escape latency: F(1,35)=31.10, P<0.001, partial η²=0.47, η² 95% CI 0.21-0.62)

findings.consequent: Navigation measures (orientation period duration, walking speed, distance travelled, path tortuosity, heading deviation, escape latency)
findings.mechanism: Learning according to either landmarks or geometry may occur at the same rate.
findings.quote: There was no effect of the cue-preference factor (orientation period duration: F(1, 35)=0.15, P=0.70; walking speed: F(1,35) =0.05, P=0.83; distance travelled: F(1, 35) = 0.61, P=0.44; path tortuosity: F(1,35)=0.93, P=0.34; heading deviation: F(1,35)=0.94, P=0.33; escape latency: F(1,35)=2.23, P=0.14) and no significant interaction for any of the navigation variables.

findings.mechanism: Preference for geometric cues manifested early during spatial learning.
findings.quote: eight subjects committed at least one rotational error during learning... These were all older adults

findings.mechanism: Visual exploration strategy associated with cue preference.
findings.quote: subjects anchoring their spatial behaviour on landmarks... spent significantly more time fixating on panels

findings.mechanism: Visual exploration strategy associated with cue preference.
findings.quote: subjects preferring geometry gazed more at the floor

findings.mechanism: Oculomotor behaviour reveals the spatial cue coding policy used by subjects.
findings.quote: Performance distribution of correct predictions (80%) suggests that gaze dynamics is indeed predictive of the spatial cue coding policy used by subjects.

findings.consequent: Number of fixations during reorientation period
findings.mechanism: More repetitive sampling of visual cues, reflecting a suboptimal visual scanning policy.
findings.quote: Older navigators produced, on average across learning trials, a significantly higher number of fixations during the reorientation period compared to young participants.

findings.consequent: Surface area covered by fixations (visual exploration)
findings.quote: older adults did not explore a larger portion of the environment, given that the surface area covered by fixations in young and older adults was equivalent.

findings.consequent: Explorative visual fixations (on floor) during reorientation
findings.mechanism: Suboptimal visual scanning policy.
findings.quote: During reorientation, older adults produced significantly fewer explorative (and more exploitative) visual fixations than young adults.

findings.consequent: Exploitative visual fixations (on panels) during reorientation
findings.mechanism: Suboptimal visual scanning policy.
findings.quote: During reorientation, older adults produced significantly fewer explorative (and more exploitative) visual fixations than young adults.

findings.consequent: Explorative visual fixations (on floor) during reorientation
findings.mechanism: Ground-dominance effect in visual exploration.
findings.quote: the geometry group produced fewer explorative visual fixations than the landmark group.
Cue preference did not lead to differences in the number of exploitative fixations during reorientation
landmark subjects tended to perform more exploitative fixations when approaching the goal.

findings.consequent: Principal Component 1 score (representing visual and cognitive functions)
findings.quote: the first component significantly discriminated subjects according to their age (F(1,31)=77.72, P<0.001, partial η²=0.73, η² 95% CI 0.52–0.82)

findings.consequent: Principal Component 1 score (representing visual and cognitive functions)
findings.mechanism: Cue preference is not well captured by general cognitive tests.
findings.quote: no clear distinction could be seen according to their cue preference (F(1,31)=0.07, P=0.79)

findings.mechanism: Impaired capacity to infer position (navigator or goal) relative to a constellation of landmarks.
findings.quote: older adults in the geometry group performed significantly worse in this test than those in the landmark group (Welch t(15.71)=2.21, P<0.05, Hedges'sg=0.82, Hedges'sg CI-0.11 to 1.83)

findings.consequent: Performance on other cognitive tests (excluding perspective-taking)
findings.quote: Results of none of the other tests correlated significantly with cue preference.

findings.mechanism: Preference for geometry is unlikely to be explained by an impaired ability to memorize features.
findings.quote: the absence of significant differences between groups in the figural memory test (Supplementary Fig. 10) suggests that the preference for geometry is unlikely to be explained by an impaired abil-ity to memorize features

findings.mechanism: Ground-dominance effect when judging distances and structure between ground and walls.
findings.quote: The apparent important role of the ground-related information for geometry-based decisions in our study is in agreement with the reported ground-dominance effect when judging distances between objects
the ground-dominance effect in visual exploration was statistically significant in both young and older subjects in the geometry group

findings.consequent: Ability to efficiently use landmarks for navigation
findings.mechanism: Inverted U-shaped dependence on landmark processing across the lifespan.
findings.quote: the capacity to efficiently use landmarks for navi-gation improves in early development, but deteriorates with ageing, giving rise to an inverted U-shaped dependence on landmark pro-cessing across the lifespan.

findings.mechanism: Suboptimal exploration-exploitation balance in visual scanning policies.
findings.quote: repetitive sampling of visual information is the main non-motor correlate of ageing in navigation, reflecting a suboptimal exploration-exploitation balance in the visual scanning policies

findings.mechanism: Inefficient sampling of visual cues requiring more fixations on the same wall panel.
findings.quote: Ageing has been associated with shrinking of the useful field of view... Therefore, an inefficient sampling of a visual cue that falls on the periphery of the visual field would require a higher number of fixations on the same wall panel
we did not find any statistical evidence for postural differences in our data.

findings.mechanism: Cue-processing deficit, specifically difficulty using landmarks.
findings.quote: ageing is associated with a specific difficulty in using allocentric navigation strategies compared to egocentric ones... If older navigators experience difficulties in using landmarks for navigation, as our results indicate, then such age-related wayfind-ing problems... may in fact be explained in terms of cue-pro-cessing deficit.

mechanisms: Impaired capacity in older adults to infer position (navigator or goal) relative to a constellation of landmarks, leading to a bias towards geometric cues.
Suboptimal exploration-exploitation balance in visual scanning policies in older adults, resulting in longer reorientation times and more repetitive sampling of visual information.
Ground-dominance effect, where ground-related information plays an important role in geometry-based decisions.
An inverted U-shaped dependence on landmark processing across the lifespan, with efficiency improving in early development but deteriorating with aging.
Cue-processing deficits (specifically difficulty using landmarks) as an explanation for age-related allocentric strategy deficits.
implementation_implications: Predicts recovery of allocentric strategies in geometrically polarized environments for older adults.
Age-induced deficits related to cue preference can be targeted by precisely tuned rehabilitation techniques and design of informative environments.
Making the geometry of an experimental environment unambiguous will improve the use of allocentric strategies in older adults.
Space design can be improved to enhance safety and quality of life in the aging population.

limitations: The assumption of an exclusive use of one type of cue (landmark or geometry) is unlikely, as subjects likely use both concurrently to some degree.

The interpretation of visual search behavior during the orientation period, especially for older adults, is not clear due to differences from classical Inhibition of Return (IoR) tasks and constrained experimental conditions.
The generalizability of IoR findings to this task is limited due to differences in experimental conditions.

paper_metadata.title: The neural correlates of the awe experience: Reduced default mode network activity during feelings of awe
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The neural correlates of the awe experience: Reduced default mode network activity during feelings of awe
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractIn the present fMRI study, we aimed to obtain insight into the key brain networks involved in the experience of awe—a complex emotion that is typically elicited by perceptually vast stimuli. Participants were presented with awe‐eliciting, positive and neutral videos, while they were instructed to get fully absorbed in the scenery or to count the number of perspective changes. By using a whole‐brain analysis we found that several brain regions that are considered part of the default mode network (DMN), including the frontal pole, the angular gyrus, and the posterior cingulate cortex, were more strongly activated in the absorption condition. But this was less the case when participants were watching awe videos. We suggest that while watching awe videos, participants were deeply immersed in the videos and that levels of self‐reflective thought were as much reduced during the awe videos, as during the perspective counting condition. In contrast, key regions of the fronto‐parietal network (FPN), including the supramarginal gyrus, the medial frontal gyrus, and the insula, were most strongly activated in the analytical condition when participants were watching awe compared to positive and neutral videos. This finding underlines the captivating, immersive, and attention‐grabbing nature of awe stimuli that is considered to be responsible for reductions in self‐reflective thought. Together these findings suggest that a key feature of the experience of awe is a reduced engagement in self‐referential processing, in line with the subjective self‐report measures (i.e., participants perceived their self to be smaller).

environmental_features: Geometric cues (e.g., boundaries, overall shape of the environment)
Potentially landmark cues (distinct objects, if used for comparison)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Multiple navigation trials over a session (e.g., 30-60 minutes)
control_conditions: Comparison between younger adults and older adults
Manipulation of cue availability or reliability (e.g., environments with varying salience of geometric vs. landmark cues)

theory_commitments.theory_name: Dual-system theory of spatial navigation (e.g., Place vs. Response learning)
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Spatial navigation relies on multiple systems (e.g., hippocampal-dependent allocentric/place learning and striatal-dependent egocentric/response learning), which may be differentially affected by aging, leading to shifts in preferred navigation strategies.

mechanism_chain.description: Age-related decline in specific brain regions and cognitive functions impairs complex spatial mapping, leading to a compensatory shift towards reliance on simpler, more robust geometric cues for navigation.

steps.to_construct: Decline in hippocampal-dependent allocentric spatial processing

steps.from_construct: Decline in hippocampal-dependent allocentric spatial processing
steps.to_construct: Reduced ability to form and utilize complex cognitive maps based on arbitrary landmarks

steps.from_construct: Reduced ability to use complex cognitive maps
steps.to_construct: Increased reliance on simpler, more robust geometric cues for navigation

instruments_used.name: Real-world navigation task (e.g., maze navigation)
instruments_used.construct: Spatial navigation strategy, preference for geometric cues, navigation performance
instruments_used.description: Participants navigate a physical environment designed to assess their use of different spatial cues.

instruments_used.name: fMRI
instruments_used.construct: Brain activity during navigation, structural integrity of brain regions (e.g., hippocampus, striatum)
